agentic.origin: The adjective ‘agentic’ predates generative AI. In current AI usage, it describes systems that pursue goals with limited direct supervision; OpenAI used ‘agentic AI systems’ in a 2023 governance paper, while later industry guidance helped standardize the modern sense around goal pursuit, planning, and action.

history.event: OpenAI published ‘Practices for Governing Agentic AI Systems,’ defining agentic AI systems as systems that can pursue complex goals with limited direct supervision.

sources.title: Practices for Governing Agentic AI Systems

ai-agent.origin: The concept of software agents is much older than modern generative AI. In current LLM usage, an AI agent generally refers to a model-centered system that directs its own process and tool use toward a user-defined goal, often operating in a loop of planning, acting, observing, and adjusting.

history.event: OpenAI’s agentic-AI governance paper described systems that can pursue complex goals with limited direct supervision.

Anthropic described an agent as an AI model that directs its own processes and tool use, repeatedly planning, acting, observing results, and adjusting until a task is complete or human input is needed.

sources.title: Practices for Governing Agentic AI Systems

ai-native.origin: ‘AI-native’ does not have a single established coinage. The phrase is used to distinguish products, companies, workflows, or systems designed around AI from the beginning from systems that add AI later as a feature. Industry usage was well established by 2023 and has since broadened across software, organizations, and operating models.

history.event: McKinsey published ‘The AI-native telco,’ using AI-native to describe organizations and operating models that integrate AI broadly rather than through isolated add-on projects.
IBM described AI-native products, companies, and workflows as designed from the ground up with AI as a core component rather than bolted on later.

sources.title: The AI-native telco: Radical transformation to thrive in turbulent times

ai-slop.origin: ‘Slop’ emerged organically as slang for unwanted or low-quality AI-generated material rather than through a single clear coinage. Simon Willison helped popularize the term in May 2024 while explicitly noting that others were already using it.

history.event: Simon Willison highlighted ‘slop’ as an emerging term for unwanted AI-generated content and compared its usefulness to ‘spam’ as a concise name for a recognizable problem.

sources.title: Slop is the new name for unwanted AI-generated content

ai-washing.origin: ‘AI washing’ adapts the older ‘washing’ metaphor, especially greenwashing, to false, vague, or exaggerated claims about artificial intelligence. A single reliable coinage event is not established in AILex's current evidence. The term became prominent as regulators began warning companies and investment firms against overstating how they use AI.

history.event: The U.S. Federal Trade Commission warned marketers against exaggerating AI capabilities or claiming products use AI when they do not, describing the underlying conduct before ‘AI washing’ became a prominent regulatory label.
SEC Chair Gary Gensler publicly used ‘AI washing’ while warning investment advisers, broker-dealers, and public companies that misleading claims about AI use may violate securities laws.

sources.title: Keep your AI claims in check
Chair Gary Gensler on AI Washing

chain-of-thought.origin: Jason Wei and colleagues introduced ‘chain-of-thought prompting’ in a 2022 paper for prompting large language models with examples that include intermediate reasoning steps.

firstKnownUse.note: The first arXiv version of ‘Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models’ introduced the named prompting method.

history.event: Wei and colleagues published the first arXiv version of the chain-of-thought prompting paper.

sources.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models

context-window.origin: ‘Context window’ is an established language-model term rather than a generative-AI coinage. It refers to the amount of input context a model can reference while generating new output, functioning as a bounded working memory distinct from the model’s training corpus.

history.event: OpenAI’s API update highlighted longer-context models alongside function calling, reflecting the term’s growing practical importance as LLM applications expanded.

sources.title: Function calling and other API updates

copilot.origin: ‘Copilot’ is an older aviation metaphor for an assistant working alongside a primary operator. In modern AI software, GitHub’s 2021 launch of GitHub Copilot was a major early use of the metaphor for an AI assistant embedded in a professional workflow, and Microsoft later expanded the label across productivity products.

history.event: GitHub launched the technical preview of GitHub Copilot and described it as an ‘AI pair programmer’ that suggests code while the developer remains in control.
Microsoft introduced Microsoft 365 Copilot as a generative-AI assistant for workplace productivity.
Microsoft unified multiple AI-assistant experiences under the Microsoft Copilot identity, reinforcing ‘copilot’ as a broad category metaphor for human-AI assistance.

sources.title: Introducing GitHub Copilot: your AI pair programmer
Introducing Microsoft 365 Copilot – your copilot for work

diffusion-model.origin: Modern diffusion-based generative modeling traces to research that applies a forward process which gradually destroys structure with noise and learns a reverse process that reconstructs data. AILex does not claim the generic phrase ‘diffusion model’ was first coined by one paper.

history.event: Sohl-Dickstein and colleagues submitted ‘Deep Unsupervised Learning using Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics,’ an influential early diffusion-based generative-model paper.

sources.title: Deep Unsupervised Learning using Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics

embedding.origin: Vector representations and embeddings have a long history in statistics, machine learning, and natural-language processing, so AILex does not assign the term to a single origin. Modern AI usage commonly refers to learned numerical representations in which semantic or structural similarity is reflected by proximity in vector space.

history.event: Mikolov and colleagues published work on efficient continuous vector representations of words, helping popularize modern neural word embeddings through word2vec.

sources.title: Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space

few-shot.origin: Few-shot learning predates modern generative AI, but the term became central to large-language-model prompting through work such as the 2020 GPT-3 paper, which evaluated task performance from a small number of demonstrations supplied in text.

history.event: The GPT-3 paper ‘Language Models are Few-Shot Learners’ documented few-shot performance using examples provided in the model's text context without gradient updates.

fine-tuning.origin: Fine-tuning is an established machine-learning term that predates the generative-AI era. It describes adapting an already pretrained model through additional training on task-specific or domain-specific data.

history.event: Fine-tuning became a common way to adapt large pretrained and foundation models to specialized behaviors and domains.

foundation-model.origin: Rishi Bommasani and colleagues introduced the term ‘foundation model’ in 2021 for models trained on broad data at scale that can be adapted to a wide range of downstream tasks.

firstKnownUse.note: The Stanford report submitted to arXiv on August 16, 2021 explicitly says, ‘We call these models foundation models.’

history.event: Stanford researchers published ‘On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models,’ naming and defining the category.

sources.title: On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models

generative-ai.origin: Generative modeling predates the current generative-AI boom, and AILex does not assign the phrase to a single inventor. In contemporary usage, generative AI refers to AI models or systems that generate new synthetic content based on patterns learned from input or training data.

history.event: The public release of ChatGPT accelerated mainstream awareness and adoption of generative AI systems.
NIST published its Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile, defining and organizing risk-management guidance for generative AI.

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile

grounding.origin: Grounding is an older AI and language-processing concept. In modern generative AI, it commonly means supplying or connecting a model to trusted external information so its response can be rooted in evidence rather than generated only from model parameters.

history.event: Google Cloud described grounding as connecting large language models with sources of truth and distinguished RAG as one specific grounding technique.

sources.title: How Vertex AI grounding helps build more reliable models

hallucination.origin: ‘Hallucination’ has a longer history in AI than the current LLM meaning. Earlier computer-vision research used ‘hallucinate’ positively for generating plausible missing image detail. By the late 2010s, neural machine-translation research used ‘hallucination’ negatively for fluent outputs that were untethered from source material. That failure-mode sense carried into modern generative AI, where the term commonly describes plausible-looking but false, unsupported, or invented output.

history.event: Carnegie Mellon researchers Simon Baker and Takeo Kanade published the technical report ‘Hallucinating Faces,’ using hallucination for generated image detail in super-resolution.
Google researchers used ‘hallucinations’ for neural machine translations that were pathological and completely untethered from the source material, closely matching the modern failure-mode sense.

As conversational large language models became widely used, ‘hallucination’ became common public and technical shorthand for confident-looking generated claims that are false, unsupported, or fabricated.

human-in-the-loop.origin: ‘Human in the loop’ predates modern machine learning and generative AI, with long-standing use in control systems, simulation, human factors, and security. In contemporary AI, the phrase describes workflows that intentionally retain human guidance, review, labeling, correction, approval, or accountability within a machine-driven process.

history.event: Lorrie Faith Cranor published a security framework for reasoning about systems that rely on a ‘human in the loop’ for security-critical functions, demonstrating established pre-LLM use of the phrase.
A major review in Artificial Intelligence Review surveyed human-in-the-loop machine learning as an umbrella for approaches that integrate people directly into ML processes.

sources.title: A Framework for Reasoning About the Human in the Loop
Human-in-the-loop machine learning: a state of the art

inference.origin: Inference is a long-established machine-learning term that predates generative AI. It refers to using a trained model on new input to produce predictions or outputs; in LLMs, that output is typically a generated response.

large-language-model.origin: Large language models grew out of decades of statistical language modeling and neural-network research. AILex does not assign the phrase to a single coinage event; in current usage it describes very large language models trained on extensive data, typically using deep-learning architectures such as transformers.

history.event: The Transformer architecture was introduced, providing the architectural basis for many later large language models.
The GPT-3 paper demonstrated broad few-shot capabilities at 175 billion parameters and helped establish the modern scale-driven LLM era.

mcp.origin: Anthropic introduced and open-sourced the Model Context Protocol as an open standard for connecting AI assistants to external data sources and tools.

history.event: Anthropic publicly introduced MCP, its specification and SDKs, local server support in Claude Desktop, and an open-source repository of MCP servers.

meat-proxy.origin: Niklas Gruhn introduced the AI-era expression ‘meat proxy’ in an August 3, 2026 essay criticizing the practice of blindly relaying AI output to other people without reading, validating, or adding judgment.

firstKnownUse.note: Gruhn's essay is the documented naming event for the current AI-era sense.

history.event: Niklas Gruhn published ‘Don't be a meat proxy,’ defining the behavior as acting as an unnecessary human relay between another person and an AI system.
Simon Willison amplified the phrase the same day and explicitly described Gruhn as coining an excellent new term for people who blindly copy and paste AI output to peers.

model-collapse.origin: Researchers led by Ilia Shumailov and Zakhar Shumaylov used ‘model collapse’ for the degenerative process that can occur when generations of generative models are recursively trained on model-generated data.

history.event: Nature published ‘AI models collapse when trained on recursively generated data,’ defining model collapse and reporting experiments across language models and other generative models.

sources.title: AI models collapse when trained on recursively generated data

multimodal.origin: ‘Multimodal’ predates modern generative AI and broadly describes systems that work across multiple forms of information. In current AI usage, multimodal models can understand or generate combinations of text, images, audio, video, code, or other modalities.

history.event: OpenAI documented GPT-4V as adding image input to GPT-4 and described multimodal LLMs as extending language-only systems with additional modalities.
Google introduced Gemini as a model family built from the ground up to be multimodal across text, code, audio, images, and video.

sources.title: Introducing Gemini: Google’s most capable AI model yet

prompt-engineering.origin: The practice of deliberately designing prompts grew rapidly with large pretrained language models, but the exact phrase ‘prompt engineering’ does not have a single confidently established coinage. Early research often used neighboring language such as ‘prompt programming’; by the early 2020s, prompt engineering became the common label for systematically shaping instructions, examples, context, and constraints to influence model behavior.

history.event: Reynolds and McDonell published ‘Prompt Programming for Large Language Models,’ documenting systematic methods for controlling GPT-3 with natural-language prompts, including metaprompts and zero-shot prompting.

sources.title: Prompt Programming for Large Language Models: Beyond the Few-Shot Paradigm

prompt-injection.origin: Simon Willison coined the term ‘prompt injection’ in September 2022 after Riley Goodside demonstrated attacks that caused GPT-3 to follow malicious instructions embedded in user input.

firstKnownUse.note: Willison's post naming the attack pattern.

history.event: Riley Goodside demonstrated malicious inputs that overrode earlier GPT-3 instructions; Simon Willison published ‘Prompt injection attacks against GPT-3’ and named the pattern prompt injection.
Willison described why adding more AI-based filtering did not provide a dependable security guarantee against prompt injection.

sources.title: You can’t solve AI security problems with more AI

rag.origin: The term Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) was introduced in a 2020 research paper by Patrick Lewis and coauthors for models that combine parametric language-model memory with retrieved non-parametric memory.

firstKnownUse.note: Date of the arXiv submission for the paper that introduced the RAG formulation and name.

history.event: Lewis and coauthors submitted ‘Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks,’ introducing the RAG name and model formulation.
The work was published at NeurIPS 2020.

sources.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks

reasoning-model.origin: Reasoning as an AI capability long predates current generative systems, and ‘reasoning model’ does not have a single clear origin. The modern product category gained prominence in 2024 when OpenAI introduced o1-preview as a model series trained to spend more time reasoning before responding.

history.event: OpenAI introduced o1-preview, describing a new series of models designed to spend more time thinking before responding and to perform better on complex reasoning tasks in science, coding, and mathematics.

rlhf.origin: Reinforcement learning from human feedback combines reinforcement-learning methods with human judgments or preferences to help define what behavior should be rewarded. The approach has roots before modern LLMs; AILex does not claim that the acronym RLHF itself originated in the 2017 paper commonly associated with the modern method.

history.event: Christiano and colleagues published ‘Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences,’ demonstrating complex behaviors learned from human preference feedback.
OpenAI's InstructGPT paper showed how human demonstrations and preference rankings could be used to align a large language model with user intent, helping popularize RLHF in the LLM era.

sources.title: Deep reinforcement learning from human preferences
Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback

semantic-search.origin: Semantic search predates modern generative AI and grew from information-retrieval and natural-language-processing efforts to search by meaning rather than exact lexical matching. Its current AI usage often combines embeddings with vector similarity techniques.

history.event: Embedding-based vector search made semantic search a common building block in modern AI retrieval and RAG systems.

sources.title: What is semantic search, and how does it work?

shadow-ai.origin: ‘Shadow AI’ extends the established enterprise-technology concept of ‘shadow IT’ to artificial-intelligence tools and services used without organizational approval, visibility, governance, or oversight. The expression grew alongside employee adoption of public generative-AI tools, but AILex does not currently identify a single defensible coinage event.

history.event: Enterprise reporting increasingly described organizations struggling with employees' unsanctioned generative-AI use, paralleling the long-standing shadow-IT problem.
IBM published a formal explainer defining shadow AI as unsanctioned AI-tool use by employees or end users without IT approval or oversight.

sources.title: IT leaders grapple with shadow AI

synthetic-content.origin: ‘Synthetic content’ is a broad policy and media term rather than a generative-AI coinage. In the current AI era, it refers to information or media significantly generated or modified by algorithms, including AI. The category includes text, images, audio, video, and other media and is broader than deliberately deceptive content such as deepfakes.

history.event: The U.S. Executive Order on Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence formally defined synthetic content as information such as images, videos, audio, and text that has been significantly modified or generated by algorithms, including AI.
The U.S. AI Safety Institute identified synthetic-content risks as an AI-safety research priority while emphasizing that synthetic content also has benign and beneficial uses.

sources.title: Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence

sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.title: Frontier Research on Mitigating Risks from Synthetic Content: A Call to Action

system-prompt.origin: The practice of giving software systems privileged or application-level instructions predates current LLMs, and AILex does not assign ‘system prompt’ to a single coinage. In modern generative AI, the term refers to instructions supplied by the model developer or application layer that establish behavior or context before ordinary user input.

history.event: Chat-based LLM APIs made role-separated instructions, including system-level messages, a mainstream application-development pattern.

token.origin: Tokens are an established concept in computing and natural-language processing, not a generative-AI coinage. In language models, tokenization divides text into the units the model processes, and those units may be whole words, word pieces, characters, punctuation, or other text fragments depending on the tokenizer.

tool-calling.origin: The broader idea of software invoking external functions predates LLMs. In modern generative AI, tool calling grew out of capabilities often first exposed as ‘function calling,’ where models produce structured requests that applications use to invoke external APIs or tools.

history.event: OpenAI announced function calling for GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 Turbo, allowing models to choose functions and emit structured arguments so applications could connect model outputs to external tools and APIs.

sources.title: Function calling and other API updates

transformer.origin: Ashish Vaswani and colleagues introduced the Transformer architecture in the 2017 paper ‘Attention Is All You Need,’ proposing a sequence-processing architecture based on attention mechanisms rather than recurrence or convolution.

firstKnownUse.note: The first arXiv version of ‘Attention Is All You Need’ introduced the architecture as ‘the Transformer.’

history.event: ‘Attention Is All You Need’ introduced the Transformer architecture.

vector-database.origin: Vector databases developed from established work in vector similarity search, nearest-neighbor indexing, and specialized data systems. AILex does not assign the modern product category to one inventor. In current AI applications, the term commonly refers to databases optimized to store, index, and query vector embeddings.

history.event: Vector databases became a prominent component of generative-AI application stacks as embeddings, semantic search, and retrieval-augmented generation became widely used.

vibe-coding.origin: Andrej Karpathy introduced the phrase ‘vibe coding’ in a February 2, 2025 social-media post describing a highly AI-directed style of building software in which the developer focuses on outcomes and may pay little attention to the generated code.

firstKnownUse.note: Karpathy's post is widely credited with introducing the term.

history.event: Andrej Karpathy posted ‘There’s a new kind of coding I call vibe coding,’ describing a workflow centered on conversational prompting, accepting generated changes, and focusing on whether the result works.
Merriam-Webster added a dictionary entry for ‘vibe coding,’ documenting the term's 2025 first known use and Karpathy attribution.

wrapper.origin: ‘Wrapper’ is an established software term for a layer placed around another component. After the rise of foundation-model APIs, ‘AI wrapper’ and ‘LLM wrapper’ became informal startup and developer language for applications whose core model intelligence comes from an external provider while the application adds interface, workflow, context, or other product layers. The label can be neutral or dismissive depending on how much additional value is implied.

history.event: As products built on commercial foundation-model APIs proliferated, ‘wrapper’ became common shorthand in startup discussions for applications layered over models such as GPT, often in debates about differentiation and defensibility.

zero-shot.origin: Zero-shot learning predates modern generative AI. The term appeared in machine-learning research by 2009 for systems that classify or predict categories omitted from training. In modern LLM prompting, zero-shot describes asking a model to perform a task without first supplying worked examples in the prompt.

firstKnownUse.note: The 2009 Palatucci et al. paper is an early documented use of the term ‘zero-shot learning’; AILex does not claim it is necessarily the absolute first use.

history.event: Palatucci, Pomerleau, Hinton, and Mitchell published ‘Zero-Shot Learning with Semantic Output Codes,’ formalizing a learning setting where a classifier predicts novel output values omitted from training.
The GPT-3 paper used zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot evaluation to describe language-model task performance with zero, one, or a small number of demonstrations in context.

sources.title: Zero-Shot Learning with Semantic Output Codes

pretraining.origin: Pretraining predates the current generative-AI era. It became central to modern language-model development through approaches that first learn broad representations from large unlabeled corpora and then adapt those representations to downstream tasks.

history.event: The BERT paper described pre-training deep bidirectional representations from unlabeled text before fine-tuning on downstream language tasks.

sources.title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding

neural-network.origin: Artificial neural networks grew from mid-20th-century efforts to model computation using simplified neuron-like units. McCulloch and Pitts described a mathematical model of neural activity in 1943, and Rosenblatt's perceptron later became one of the earliest implemented learning networks.

history.event: Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts published an influential mathematical model of neural activity.
Frank Rosenblatt published the perceptron, an early learning system that became foundational to neural-network history.

sources.title: The Perceptron: A Probabilistic Model for Information Storage and Organization in the Brain

deep-learning.origin: Deep learning refers to machine learning with multilayer neural networks. The phrase existed before today's neural-network usage, while the modern sense became established as multilayer networks and improved training methods produced major gains in vision, speech, and other tasks.

history.event: Deep convolutional neural networks achieved a major ImageNet breakthrough, helping accelerate modern adoption of deep learning.

sources.title: ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks

machine-learning.origin: Machine learning became an established AI research term in the 1950s. Arthur Samuel's 1959 checkers paper is widely associated with early use and popularization of the phrase for systems that improve performance through experience.

firstKnownUse.note: Arthur Samuel's IBM paper is a well-documented early use and is widely credited with coining or popularizing the term, though AILex does not claim it is provably the absolute first occurrence.

history.event: Arthur Samuel published ‘Some Studies in Machine Learning Using the Game of Checkers’ in the IBM Journal of Research and Development.

sources.publisher: IBM Journal of Research and Development
sources.title: Some Studies in Machine Learning Using the Game of Checkers

artificial-general-intelligence.origin: Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) became a distinct research label in the mid-2000s for work aimed at broad, general-purpose machine intelligence rather than narrow task-specific systems. The concept remains disputed because there is no universally accepted operational definition or threshold for achieving AGI.

firstKnownUse.note: Goertzel and Pennachin's edited volume is an early landmark use that explicitly framed and named the field as Artificial General Intelligence.

history.event: Ben Goertzel and Cassio Pennachin edited the volume ‘Artificial General Intelligence,’ presenting AGI as a distinct research area.
The first Conference on Artificial General Intelligence was held, further institutionalizing the label.

sources.title: The First Conference on Artificial General Intelligence

small-language-model.origin: Small Language Model (SLM) emerged as a practical category label during the rapid expansion of generative AI to distinguish comparatively compact language models from cloud-scale LLMs. The category is relative rather than defined by one universal parameter threshold.

history.event: Microsoft Research described Phi-2 as part of a suite of small language models, helping establish SLM as a widely used category label.

sources.title: Phi-2: The surprising power of small language models

vision-language-model.origin: Vision-language models developed from multimodal research that learns relationships between images and text. The VLM label became common as large-scale image-text pretraining enabled one model to perform multiple visual-language tasks and zero-shot transfer.

history.event: A major survey documented Vision-Language Models as an established research category and summarized their architectures, pretraining, transfer learning, and zero-shot capabilities.

sources.title: Vision-Language Models for Vision Tasks: A Survey

parameters.origin: Parameter is an established mathematical and machine-learning term rather than an AI-era coinage. In trained models, parameters are numerical values learned from data, commonly including weights and biases.

model-weights.origin: Weight is an established neural-network and statistical-model term. In modern AI, model weights are the learned numerical connection strengths that make up a large share of a model's trainable parameters.

training-data.origin: Training data is an established machine-learning term for the examples used during model training. In generative AI, the phrase has gained broader public importance because dataset composition affects capability, bias, privacy, intellectual-property questions, and model behavior.

history.event: NIST's adversarial machine-learning terminology formally described attacks that target or control training data, reflecting its central role in AI security and governance.

synthetic-data.origin: Synthetic data predates generative AI and broadly refers to artificial data created to preserve useful characteristics of real or seed data. Modern generative systems greatly expanded the scale and variety of synthetic data used for model training and evaluation.

attention.origin: Attention mechanisms were developed in neural sequence modeling before the Transformer. They allow models to compute weighted relationships between parts of an input instead of compressing all relevant information into a single fixed representation.

history.event: ‘Attention Is All You Need’ showed that a high-performing sequence model could be built around attention mechanisms without recurrent or convolutional layers.

self-attention.origin: Self-attention is an attention mechanism in which positions within one sequence attend to other positions in that same sequence. It became foundational to modern language models through the Transformer architecture.

history.event: The Transformer paper used self-attention as the central mechanism for relating positions within input and output sequences.

prompt.origin: Prompt is an older computing and interaction term that became central to generative AI as pretrained language models began accepting natural-language input to condition their behavior. AILex does not assign a single generative-AI coinage event.

history.event: Large language models such as GPT-3 helped make natural-language prompting a primary way to adapt model behavior without parameter updates.

user-prompt.origin: User prompt is a practical role-based label used in chat and model APIs for input attributed to the end user. The wording varies by platform, so AILex treats it as a functional category rather than a coined term.

history.event: OpenAI API documentation defines user messages as end-user messages containing prompts or additional context and places them below developer or system instructions in the instruction hierarchy.

developer-prompt.origin: Developer prompt reflects the modern API practice of separating application-level instructions from end-user input. OpenAI's newer model APIs use the developer role for instructions that take precedence over user messages, while other platforms may use different names for the same architectural idea.

history.event: OpenAI API documentation describes developer instructions as higher priority than user instructions and recommends the developer role for newer models where older APIs often used system messages.

sources.title: OpenAI API Reference: developer and user roles

prompt-template.origin: Prompt templates are an application-development pattern that applies ordinary software templating to reusable AI prompts. The pattern does not have a single defensible AI-era coinage event.

history.event: Google Cloud documentation describes prompt templates as prompts with replaceable variables that can be reused with different prompt data.

prompt-chaining.origin: Prompt chaining developed as a practical way to decompose generative-AI tasks into sequential model calls. AILex does not assign a single coinage event because similar multi-stage pipelines appeared across early LLM tooling and prompting practice.

history.event: Google's machine-learning glossary defines prompt chaining as using the output of one prompt as the input to another.

one-shot.origin: One-shot learning predates large language models. In modern prompting, the term refers to providing one demonstration in the model's context before the target query. The GPT-3 paper formalized one-shot as one of its principal in-context evaluation settings.

history.event: The GPT-3 paper evaluated one-shot learning as an in-context setting with a single demonstration and no gradient updates.

in-context-learning.origin: In-context learning describes adaptation that occurs through information supplied in a model's current input rather than through weight updates. The 2020 GPT-3 paper made the concept a central part of large-language-model evaluation and usage.

history.event: The GPT-3 paper described and evaluated in-context learning across zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot settings without gradient updates or fine-tuning.

context-engineering.origin: Context engineering emerged as a broader companion to prompt engineering as agentic systems required developers to manage not only instructions but also tools, retrieved data, message history, memory, and other state within a finite context window. Anthropic described the term as having come to prominence by 2025 rather than attributing it to a single inventor.

history.event: Anthropic published ‘Effective context engineering for AI agents,’ distinguishing context engineering from prompt engineering and framing it as curation of the full token context used during inference.

sources.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents

prompt-caching.origin: Prompt caching is an optimization pattern in which model providers reuse computation for repeated prompt prefixes or context. OpenAI introduced automatic Prompt Caching in its API in October 2024, while similar caching capabilities have also existed on other model platforms.

history.event: OpenAI introduced automatic Prompt Caching for supported API models, reducing latency and input cost when prompts reuse previously seen token prefixes.

chunking.origin: Chunking is an older information-processing technique. In modern RAG systems, it commonly refers to splitting documents into smaller indexable and retrievable units so relevant passages can be found and supplied to a model efficiently.

history.event: Google Cloud announced document-chunking improvements for Vertex AI Search and described chunking as a way to improve relevance and reduce computational load for RAG.

retrieval.origin: Information retrieval is a field much older than generative AI. In contemporary AI systems, retrieval commonly refers to selecting the information most relevant to a query so it can be searched, ranked, or supplied to a generative model.

history.event: The RAG paper combined neural retrieval with generation and helped make retrieval a central component of modern knowledge-grounded language-model systems.

sources.title: Vertex AI APIs for building search and RAG experiences
Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks

reranking.origin: Reranking is an established information-retrieval technique that predates generative AI. In RAG and semantic-search pipelines, it usually refers to applying a second-stage model or scoring method to reorder an initially retrieved candidate set by relevance.

history.event: Google Cloud documented reranking as a step after retrieval that can improve which chunks or documents are supplied to an LLM for grounding.

sources.title: Improve search and RAG quality with ranking API
